name: Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection

likely: Candida species (colonization common, true infection less so)
possible: Polymicrobial flora, especially with long-term catheterization
pathogens.why: Catheter-associated UTI involves a broader and more resistant organism spectrum than uncomplicated cystitis due to biofilm formation on the catheter surface and selection pressure from prior antibiotic exposure, with polymicrobial infection common in long-term catheterization.

investigations.test: Urine culture (from newly placed catheter if replacing, or freshly collected sample)
investigations.why: Essential given the high resistance burden and biofilm-related polymicrobial colonization in this population — guides definitive therapy.
CA-UTI can be a source of bacteremia/urosepsis; positive cultures confirm systemic involvement.
Baseline assessment, particularly relevant if upper tract involvement (pyelonephritis) is suspected.

reason: Fever (often the only symptom, since dysuria is typically absent or unreliable with a catheter in place) in a catheterized patient, without an alternative explanation, is consistent with catheter-associated UTI. Critically, this diagnosis requires the presence of symptoms/signs attributable to UTI — asymptomatic bacteriuria in a catheterized patient is extremely common and should NOT be treated with antibiotics.

clinicalPearls: CAUTI is diagnosed only when localizing urinary and/or systemic symptoms (e.g., fever) are present together with pyuria and bacteriuria; bacteriuria and pyuria alone do not establish the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1090).

Because the catheter is a conduit for bacterial entry, bacteriuria is essentially inevitable with catheterization, so an abnormal urinalysis alone should not be the endpoint of evaluating a febrile catheterized patient (Harrison 22e p.1090).
The accepted bacteriuria threshold for CAUTI is at least 10^3 colony-forming units per mL of urine (Harrison 22e p.1090).
Typical UTI features (pain, urgency, dysuria, fever, peripheral leukocytosis) have lower predictive value in catheterized patients than in non-catheterized patients (Harrison 22e p.1090).

The catheter should be exchanged or, if feasible, removed during treatment to clear biofilm-associated organisms; ideally the exchange precedes urine culture collection so results reflect bladder rather than catheter-wall microbiology (Harrison 22e p.1094).

Very high pyuria levels are common with urinary stasis (e.g., end-stage renal disease, obstructed catheters) and the degree of pyuria should not influence the distinction between asymptomatic bacteriuria and true UTI in an asymptomatic patient (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Candiduria is common in catheterized patients, especially after antimicrobial therapy for CAUTI or inappropriate treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria; removal of the catheter alone resolves candiduria in over a third of asymptomatic cases (Harrison 22e pp.1088, 1095).

Urine nitrite is detectable only with Enterobacterales and adequate accumulation, so it can be falsely negative with non-Enterobacterales pathogens (e.g., enterococci, Pseudomonas, Candida) that are prominent in CAUTI (Harrison 22e pp.1090-1091).
harrison.pathophysiology: Urinary catheters and other foreign bodies (stones, stents, nephrostomy tubes) provide an inert surface for bacterial colonization and formation of a persistent biofilm, and catheterization dramatically increases bacterial entry into the urinary tract. The catheter serves as a conduit allowing organisms to ascend into the bladder, making bacteriuria nearly universal during catheterization. Biofilm on the catheter shelters organisms and acts as a nidus for reinfection, which is why catheter exchange or removal is central to clearing infection. The microbiology is more diverse than in uncomplicated cystitis; while E. coli remains predominant, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, enterococci, Staphylococcus aureus, and Candida are important additional pathogens (Harrison 22e pp.1087-1088, 1094).
additionalDifferentials: Asymptomatic bacteriuria / catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria (positive culture without localizing or systemic symptoms attributable to UTI)
Complicated UTI extending beyond the bladder (prostatitis, pyelonephritis, bacteremia)
Candiduria representing colonization rather than true infection in a catheterized patient
Other infectious or noninfectious source of fever or altered mentation in a catheterized patient, which must be systematically excluded before attributing symptoms to CAUTI
infectionMimics: Candida colonization of the catheter/urine without invasive infection
Another concurrent infection (e.g., respiratory, intra-abdominal, bloodstream) causing the fever or systemic findings
nonInfectiousMimics: Delirium from non-infectious causes (e.g., metabolic, medication-related) in an older patient, mistaken for UTI-related encephalopathy
Pyuria due to urinary stasis from an obstructed catheter rather than active infection
Hematuria or local irritation from catheter trauma
additionalInvestigations: Urine culture collected from a freshly placed catheter (after exchanging/removing the indwelling catheter) to reflect bladder rather than biofilm microbiology, with susceptibilities to guide therapy
Urine dipstick (nitrite, leukocyte esterase) and microscopic urinalysis, interpreted with awareness that pyuria and bacteriuria are expected in catheterized patients
Systematic workup to exclude alternative infectious and non-infectious causes of fever or altered mental status before settling on CAUTI
redFlags: Fever, rigors, nausea/vomiting, or flank/costovertebral angle pain suggesting infection has extended beyond the bladder (pyelonephritis or bloodstream)
Signs of sepsis in a catheterized patient with systemic symptoms
Isolation of S. aureus from urine, which should prompt consideration of concomitant bacteremia
Persistent fever and/or bacteremia despite appropriate therapy, suggesting renal/perinephric abscess or obstruction requiring drainage
harrison.prognosis: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in catheterized and elderly patients but does not itself increase risk of infection or death, which argues against treating it. In the absence of anatomic abnormalities (e.g., reflux, obstruction), recurrent urinary infection does not lead to chronic pyelonephritis or renal failure; however, with underlying renal abnormalities such as obstructing stones, infection can accelerate renal parenchymal damage. A randomized trial found more relapses with 3 versus 14 days of therapy, supporting longer treatment than for uncomplicated cystitis (Harrison 22e pp.1094-1095).
pitfalls: Treating catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria: apart from pregnancy (and pre-urologic-procedure screening), urine culture and treatment are not indicated for asymptomatic catheterized patients, and treating it does not reduce subsequent infection (Harrison 22e pp.1147, 1095).

Attributing nonspecific symptoms such as confusion in an elderly catheterized patient to bacteriuria without excluding other time-sensitive causes of delirium, leading to premature diagnostic closure (Harrison 22e pp.1089, 1147).
Improper treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria followed by repeat 'test-of-cure' cultures, driving a vicious cycle of escalating antimicrobial use and resistance (Harrison 22e p.1147).
Sending urine cultures in catheterized patients lacking signs/symptoms of UTI (poor diagnostic stewardship), which promotes overdiagnosis and overtreatment (Harrison 22e pp.1089, 1147).

Sampling urine through the existing biofilm-laden catheter rather than from a newly placed catheter, yielding culture results that reflect the catheter wall rather than the bladder (Harrison 22e p.1094).
Routinely using antimicrobial (silver- or nitrofurazone-impregnated) catheters to prevent CAUTI, which has not shown significant clinical benefit (Harrison 22e p.1094).
harrison.severityClassification: CAUTI falls within the complicated UTI category, defined by infection in the setting of intermittent or indwelling urinary catheterization. Severity ranges from localized symptomatic infection to infection extending beyond the bladder (pyelonephritis, bacteremia) signaled by fever, rigors, flank pain, and systemic toxicity (Harrison 22e pp.1086-1087, 1089).
